name: PostgreSQL
baseline: MySQL 8.0 (InnoDB, sysbench; MySQL figures are Oracle's published 'extreme config' sysbench numbers as tabulated in the pgtpc repo)
workload: sysbench oltp_point_select, oltp_read_only, oltp_read_write and oltp_update_non_index on 8 tables of 10M-50M rows, PostgreSQL 14.5 with a 'NOT FOR PRODUCTION' config (fsync off, synchronous_commit off, full_page_writes off, shared_buffers 128GB) on an AWS c5d.metal with threads forced to 48, versus MySQL 8.0 numbers from a 48-core run with the equivalent durability-off settings.
claimed_speedup: Queries per second, PostgreSQL 48 threads vs MySQL 8.0 48C, as tabulated on the benchmark page: oltp_point_select 1,814,404 vs 1,050,000 (1.73x, derived from page data); oltp_read_only 941,694 vs 920,000 (1.02x, derived); oltp_update_non_index 269,233 vs 240,000 (1.12x, derived); oltp_read_write 722,907 vs 900,000 (MySQL 1.25x faster, derived). At 96 threads PostgreSQL reaches 2,332,928 point-select QPS and 910,554 read_write QPS. The repo's own summary: 'PGSQL has a similar write performance and significantly better read performance to MySQL.'
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 14.5; build compiler and flags not stated. initdb with LATIN1 and C locale, postgresql.conf and sysbench commands are listed in sysbench/aws.c5d.metal.extreme.md of the benchmark repo.
hardware: PostgreSQL side: AWS c5d.metal, 96 vCPU at 3.6 GHz (per the Compare table), 192 GB, 4x 900 GB ephemeral NVMe, CPU model not stated. MySQL side (Oracle's published run): 48 cores at 2.7 GHz, 172 GB, 2x Intel Optane P4800X.
stars_or_usage: 22.4k stars (GitHub mirror of the official git repository)
tradeoffs: Client-server RDBMS with process-per-connection backends, MVCC with vacuum, WAL and a full SQL planner; not an embedded key-value engine (filed under embedded-kv only because storage-and-data has no relational category in wave 6, SQLite being the nearest baseline). Needs a running server and tuning (shared_buffers, WAL settings) to reach the quoted rates.
caveats: The head-to-head is not same-machine: the PostgreSQL rows were run by the pgtpc author on c5d.metal (PostgreSQL 14.5), while the MySQL 8.0 rows are Oracle's own published sysbench results (MySQL official benchmark page and a MySQL performance blog, both blocked from this session), on a different 48-core 2.7 GHz box with Optane storage. Both sides use durability-off 'extreme' settings (pgtpc says MySQL's page turns off checksum, doublewrite, binlog, PFS and fsync; PostgreSQL has fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes off) and are not production configurations. MySQL wins the oltp_read_write row at 48 threads, so the win is workload dependent. No compiler, flags or CPU model, so not tier A; the repo has no LICENSE file and its last commit is 2022-08-22. Corroboration, same direction: a HammerDB TPROC-C discussion on a laptop (https://github.com/TPC-Council/HammerDB/discussions/259; i7-1165G7, 16 GB, Docker 'latest' images limited to 12 GB, 100 warehouses, 1 virtual user) reports about 14,000 NOPM for PostgreSQL vs about 3,800 for MySQL, with the HammerDB maintainer replying that PostgreSQL does perform better on this single-threaded test but that the gap is smaller on servers; database versions are not stated. A small Takeruso/rdbms-performance-comparison repo (sysbench 10 threads, 60 s, Docker on WSL) shows near parity in transactions (about 20,963 PostgreSQL vs 20,845 MySQL) with PostgreSQL at 4.77 ms vs 28.78 ms average latency. A DoltHub 2024 blog post (Postgres 15.5 vs MySQL 8.0.35, point select median 0.14 ms vs 0.18 ms, read_write 4.33 ms vs 8.58 ms) was seen only as a WebSearch result summary and could not be opened. No PostgreSQL vs SQLite number was found.

name: MySQL
baseline: PostgreSQL 14.5 (sysbench, PostgreSQL run on a different, larger machine)
workload: sysbench oltp_read_write on 8 tables of 10M rows, MySQL 8.0 'extreme config' (checksum, doublewrite, binlog, performance schema and fsync off, latin1) on a 48-core 2.7 GHz box with Optane storage, versus PostgreSQL 14.5 run by the pgtpc author with threads forced to 48 on an AWS c5d.metal.
claimed_speedup: Queries per second as tabulated on the benchmark page: oltp_read_write MySQL 900,000 vs PostgreSQL 722,907 at 48 threads (1.25x, derived from page data). PostgreSQL is ahead or level on the other rows: oltp_point_select 1,050,000 vs 1,814,404; oltp_read_only 920,000 vs 941,694; oltp_update_non_index 240,000 vs 269,233; and at 96 threads PostgreSQL's read_write is 910,554 (parity). The page's own summary favours PostgreSQL: 'PGSQL has a similar write performance and significantly better read performance to MySQL.'
hardware: MySQL side (Oracle's published run): 48 cores at 2.7 GHz, 172 GB, 2x Intel Optane P4800X, CPU model not stated. PostgreSQL side: AWS c5d.metal 96 vCPU at 3.6 GHz, 192 GB, 4x 900 GB ephemeral NVMe.
tradeoffs: Client-server RDBMS (InnoDB), not an embedded key-value engine; filed under embedded-kv only because storage-and-data has no relational category in wave 6. GPL-2.0 with additional linking permissions for separately licensed components such as OpenSSL (LICENSE file); Oracle also sells commercial editions. The quoted rates need the durability-off configuration.
caveats: Weak and mixed evidence, kept for completeness: the only MySQL-favourable row (oltp_read_write at 48 threads) compares Oracle's own published MySQL 8.0 numbers with a PostgreSQL run on a different machine, and the page's author (a PostgreSQL advocate) frames the table as PostgreSQL winning reads. MySQL loses oltp_point_select by about 1.7x and is level or behind on the other rows. Both sides are durability-off 'extreme' configs, not production settings. Oracle's original sources (mysql.com benchmarks page and a MySQL performance blog) were not reachable from this session, so the MySQL figures are quoted only as tabulated in pgtpc. Other head-to-heads found favour PostgreSQL: a HammerDB TPROC-C discussion (https://github.com/TPC-Council/HammerDB/discussions/259, laptop, 1 virtual user, about 3,800 NOPM for MySQL vs about 14,000 for PostgreSQL, versions unstated) and a DoltHub 2024 sysbench latency post seen only as a search summary. The mysql-server repo itself carries no performance claims or benchmark files.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: oz123/awesome-c list, Database section ('The world's most popular open source database'), then WebSearch 'PostgreSQL vs SQLite benchmark github pgbench ...' which surfaced github.com/Vonng/pgtpc (MySQL Compare table in sysbench/ref-mysql.md)

name: ODB
baseline: Hand-coded ADO.NET SqlDataReader and Dapper (C#/.NET micro-ORM), using Dapper's published 500-object SELECT benchmark
workload: Dapper's benchmark reimplemented in C++: load 500 randomly chosen post objects (Stack Overflow-style posts table) one by one, timing 500 iterations.
claimed_speedup: From the blog post's search-result text (snippet only): ODB with MySQL 5.1.49 on Linux 24 ms per 500 iterations vs 47 ms for hand-coded C# SqlDataReader and 49 ms for Dapper (about 2x, derived from snippet data). Follow-up post (Jan 2012): ODB 27 ms with PostgreSQL 9.0.4, 24 ms with MySQL 5.1.49, 7 ms with SQLite 3.7.5 per 500 iterations.
stars_or_usage: 65 stars on the GitHub mirror; long-standing C++ ORM with MySQL, SQLite, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server backends
tradeoffs: Code-generating ORM: a separate ODB compiler processes annotated C++ headers into persistence code; an ORM mapping layer rather than a raw client. The repo file list shows GPLv2, GPLv3, NCUEL and Unlicense files and the README defers to the product page for terms, so check the licence split before closed-source use.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: codesynthesis.com is blocked from this session (DNS ENOTFOUND for WebFetch, CONNECT 403 for curl), so the benchmark page was never opened; the figures come from WebSearch result summaries of the 2011-04-06 blog post and a January 2012 follow-up, and the URL above is one the search returned, not one opened. The C# figures (47 ms, 49 ms) are Dapper's published numbers from a different machine and a different database (SQL Server), not a same-machine run, so the 2x is indicative only. Roughly 15-year-old numbers on MySQL 5.1, PostgreSQL 9.0 and SQLite 3.7, hardware not captured. The repo itself carries no benchmark claims, and no comparison against another C++ ORM (sqlpp11, SOCI, sqlite_orm, Wt::Dbo) was found. The ODB product page was also unreachable, so the licence is taken from the GitHub mirror's file listing.
